newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Siemens on track despite Q1 profit fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Siemens on track despite Q1 profit fall.

text.p: German engineering giant Siemens AG said on Tuesday that first-quarter group net profit fell five percent as a result of falling memory chip prices and weak domestic demand.
But the company said its forecast of unchanged profit for the 1996/97 business year remained intact, despite the first quarter decline.
Group net profit fell in the first quarter, ending December 31, to 478 million marks ($289.5 million) from 503 million marks in the same period a year earlier.
"The numbers are in line with the forecast," a Siemens spokesman told Reuters from company headquarters in Munich.
But analysts called the results "slightly disappointing" because Siemens said in November profit would be unchanged in 1996/97.
"A five percent drop is not unchanged," said Hans Peter Wodniok, a Credit Lyonnais analyst in Frankfurt.
"The first quarter was not that bad, but if profit falls five percent for the full year, that would clearly be a bigger disappointment."
Siemens shares were up 46 pfennigs in pre-bourse electronic trading at 79 marks, over eight marks above their low after the company's warning of no earnings improvement in 1996/97.
In 1995/96, group net profit rose to 3.3 billion marks from 1.9 billion marks.
First quarter group sales rose six percent to 20.9 billion, while incoming orders climbed 22 percent to 27 billion marks.
Siemens said that the pickup in new orders was largely due to major projects, with growth led by energy, transport, telecommunications and information operations.
Foreign orders led the way, rising by 130 percent in the Asia-Pacific region and by 37 percent in the Americas. Orders in Germany rose eight percent to 9.5 billion marks.
International sales increased seven percent to 13 billion marks and domestic sales six percent to 7.9 billion marks.
Around two percentage points of Siemens' international growth can be attributed to the impact of the strong dollar. But the company said it expected growth to level off.
"Following the amassing of major projects in the first quarter, growth is expected to normalise for the remainder of the year," the company said.
Sales grew evenly both at home and abroad, with the group's telecommunications, power, energy, and information divisions posting double-digit rates.
Leading the growth sectors, public communication networks (ON) business saw first quarter orders rise 55 percent to 4.5 billion marks and sales climb 38 percent to 2.8 billion marks.

The KWU power generation unit, where orders rose 129 percent to 2.4 billion marks was helped by projects in Pakistan, Thailand, the United States and Taiwan. But unit revenue declined 31 percent because of falling prices.
But Siemens' industrial businesses saw declining orders, mostly due to weak demand for capital goods in Germany.
The semiconductor business, buffeted by sharp price erosion, suffered a 24 percent drop in orders, to 1.2 billion marks, and a 12 percent fall in sales to one billion marks.

Automation (AUT) orders fell five percent to 1.6 billion marks and sales two percent ot 1.4 billion marks. Industrial building systems orders slipped four percent ot 2.4 billion marks against a nine percent sales rise to 1.8 billion marks.
The concern's workforce fell to 377,000 at the end of 1996, down slightly from the end-September figure of 379,000, with some jobs being cut in Germany and added abroad.

First-quarter capital spending climbed 36 percent to two billion marks, driven higher by acquisitions. Siemens recently purchased industrial units from Switzerland's Electrowatt AG, and AEG Electrocom GmbH, a maker of postal machinery.
